facts.statement: The genus Ornithoprion was described by Rainer Zangerl in 1966.
facts.quote: authority: Zangerl, 1966

facts.statement: The only known species, Ornithoprion hertwigi, lived during the Moscovian stage of the Pennsylvanian subperiod.
facts.quote: The only known species, O. hertwigi, lived during the Moscovian stage of the Pennsylvanian subperiod

facts.statement: Fossils of Ornithoprion are preserved in black shales from the area that is now the Midwestern United States.
facts.quote: Its fossils are preserved in black shales from what became the Midwestern United States.

facts.statement: The genus Ornithoprion and its type species O. hertwigi were formally described in 1966 by paleontologist Rainer Zangerl.
facts.quote: The genus Ornithoprion and its only species, O. hertwigi, were formally described in 1966 by paleontologist Rainer Zangerl.

facts.statement: Specimen FMNH PF-2710 from the Mecca Quarry was designated as the holotype of the species.
facts.quote: Specimen FMNH PF-2710 from the Mecca Quarry was designated as the holotype

facts.statement: All known specimens of Ornithoprion are preserved in carbonaceous shale.
facts.quote: The specimens are all preserved in carbonaceous shale

facts.statement: The study of the holotype and paratypes of Ornithoprion was primarily performed using radiographic imaging.
facts.quote: study of the holotype and paratypes of Ornithoprion were primarily performed by radiographic imaging

facts.statement: The genus name Ornithoprion translates from Greek as 'bird saw', referring to the bird-like skull and saw-like lower jaw teeth.
facts.quote: Ornithoprion's genus name, which may be translated from Greek as 'bird saw', was inspired by the animal's vaguely bird-like skull and the saw-like appearance of the teeth in the lower jaw

facts.statement: The specific name hertwigi honors the German zoologist Oscar Hertwig.
facts.quote: the specific name honors German zoologist Oscar Hertwig

facts.statement: Ornithoprion was small relative to its order, with a cranium up to 10 cm long and an estimated body length of approximately 91 cm.
facts.quote: Ornithoprion was small relative to other members of its order, with a cranium length of up to 10 cm and an estimated body length of up to approximately 91 cm.

facts.statement: Most known specimens are preserved on their side and are flattened, including the holotype.
facts.quote: Most of these are preserved on their side, and all, including the holotype, are flattened.

facts.statement: The mandibular rostrum articulated with the Meckel's cartilages at a flexible joint.
facts.quote: The rostrum articulated with the Meckel's cartilages (equivalent to the mandible) at a flexible joint

facts.statement: Due to the shape of the Meckel's cartilages, the mouth of Ornithoprion was likely incapable of closing.
facts.quote: Because of the shape of the Meckel's cartilages, the mouth was likely incapable of closing.

facts.statement: The rounded shape of Ornithoprion's teeth suggests it hunted hard-shelled invertebrates.
facts.quote: The rounded shape of Ornithoprion's teeth suggests that it hunted hard-shelled invertebrates

facts.statement: Bite marks and damage on some fossils indicate that Ornithoprion was preyed upon by other carnivores.
facts.quote: bite marks and damage to some of its fossils indicate that it was in turn fed on by other carnivores.

facts.statement: Ornithoprion is classified in the order Eugeneodontiformes and the family Caseodontidae, though its classification has been debated due to its unique anatomy.
facts.quote: The classification of the genus has been the subject of debate due to its unique anatomy; it is placed in the order Eugeneodontiformes and the family Caseodontidae.

facts.statement: While Zangerl speculated that processes on the back of the cranium were a fused hyoid arch, this interpretation has been questioned by paleontologist Svend Erik Bendix-Almgreen.
facts.quote: Processes on the back of the cranium that Zangerl speculated to be a fused hyoid arch are also known,, although the interpretation of these structures as part of a hyoid arch has subsequently been questioned by paleontologist Svend Erik Bendix-Almgreen.

facts.statement: Ornithoprion had a lower jaw tooth arrangement called a tooth whorl, which looked like a saw and featured up to seven broad, rounded tooth crowns.
facts.quote: The lower dentition of Ornithoprion consisted of multiple tooth crowns extending from a connected base (or root) along the midline of the lower jaw; an arrangement which resembled a saw and is referred to as a tooth whorl.

facts.statement: Ornithoprion possessed additional rows of flattened, rod-like teeth with an uneven surface texture along the sides of its jaws.
facts.quote: Additional rows of tightly stacked, flattened teeth were also present, which were likely positioned along the lateral (side) surfaces of the jaws.

facts.statement: The side teeth of Ornithoprion formed a brick-like pattern known as a tooth pavement, similar to other Paleozoic cartilaginous fish.
facts.quote: The flattened teeth elsewhere in the lower jaws were rod-like and had an uneven surface texture. They formed a brick-like arrangement termed a "tooth pavement" similar to that of many other Paleozoic cartilaginous fish.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the attachment of Ornithoprion's upper teeth, with some researchers suggesting they attached to the underside of the cranium while others believe they attached to a fused portion of the palatoquadrates.
facts.quote: Zangerl, in both his initial description of the taxon and in later works, suggested that the upper teeth were associated directly with the underside of the cranium. Later works by Bendix-Almgreen and paleontologist Roger S. Miles have alternatively suggested that Ornithoprion's upper teeth instead attached to a previously unrecognized portion of the palatoquadrates that was fused to the cranium.

facts.statement: Ornithoprion's tooth crowns were likely made of trabecular dentin covered by an outer layer of orthodentin.
facts.quote: Based on thin sectioning, the tooth crowns of Ornithoprion are thought to have been composed primarily of trabecular dentin (a spongy form of dentin present in holocephalan fishes) with an outer coating of orthodentin.

facts.statement: Many dermal denticles on Ornithoprion fused into compound scales called polyodontode scales, featuring a single base with up to seven crowns.
facts.quote: Many of these denticles formed fused, compound structures termed polyodontode scales, which shared a single mushroom-shaped base with upwards of seven crowns emerging from it.

facts.statement: The bases of the dermal denticles in Ornithoprion may have been made of bone, unlike the dentin bases found in other cartilaginous fish.
facts.quote: However, the bases of the denticles in Ornithoprion may have uniquely been composed of bone, rather than a form of dentin like in other cartilaginous fish.

facts.statement: In 1966, Zangerl speculated that the bony rods on Ornithoprion's snout and jaw were formed by fused polyodontode scales.
facts.quote: In his 1966 description, Zangerl speculates that the reinforcing bony rods present on the snout and mandibular rostrum were formed by the compounding and fusion of polyodontode scales.

facts.statement: Ornithoprion's unfused pectoral girdles included an unpaired cartilaginous structure tentatively identified as sternal cartilage.
facts.quote: The paired left and right scapulocoracoids were unfused and had forward-angled scapular portions, as well as an unpaired cartilaginous structure which has been tentatively identified as sternal cartilage running beneath their coracoidal portions.

facts.statement: There is no evidence that Ornithoprion's fins supported defensive spines.
facts.quote: There is no indication that the fins supported defensive fin spines.

facts.statement: Ornithoprion's vertebrae were uncalcified in life, though cartilaginous structures are preserved along the spine.
facts.quote: The vertebral centra of Ornithoprion are not preserved and were uncalcified in life, although a series of cartilaginous structures are present along the path of the vertebral column.

facts.statement: Zangerl proposed that large, leaf-shaped cartilaginous structures along the spine were neural arches adapted to the unique skull morphology of Ornithoprion.
facts.quote: Zangerl suggested that these elements, which he described as large and leaf-shaped, represented the neural arches of the animal's vertebrae, and he further proposed that their shape may have been an adaptation associated with the unique morphology of the animal's skull.

facts.statement: The spinal cord of Ornithoprion was protected by a flexible notochord.
facts.quote: The spinal cord of Ornithoprion was sheathed by a flexible notochord.

facts.statement: Ornithoprion is a distant relative of living sharks, despite sometimes being referred to as a shark.
facts.quote: Though sometimes referred to as a shark, Ornithoprion is only a distant relative of living sharks (Selachii).

facts.statement: Ornithoprion was originally classified in the family Edestidae, which was traditionally placed in the order Bradyodonti or the subclass Holocephali.
facts.quote: When first described, the genus was classified in the family Edestidae, which itself was traditionally considered a member of the order (sometimes class) Bradyodonti or the equivalent subclass Holocephali.

facts.statement: Zangerl originally classified Ornithoprion and other edestids as elasmobranchs.
facts.quote: In his description of the genus, however, Zangerl classified it and other edestids as elasmobranchs.

facts.statement: Roger S. Miles tentatively placed Ornithoprion in Holocephali but suggested its similarities to edestids resulted from convergent evolution due to differences in gill anatomy, tooth histology, and palatoquadrates.
facts.quote: In the 1971 edition of Paleozoic Fishes, Roger S. Miles considered the genus to be of uncertain position within Chondrichthyes, and only tentatively placed it within Holocephali. He suggested that Ornithoprions similarities with edestids may be the result of convergent evolution (meaning they developed independently) because of differences in the anatomy of the gills, the tooth histology, and the palatoquadrates.

facts.statement: In 1981, Zangerl reclassified Ornithoprion into the family Caseodontidae, superfamily Caseodontoidea, and order Eugeneodontiformes.
facts.quote: In a 1981 book, Zangerl considered Ornithoprion a member of the new family Caseodontidae, as part of the larger superfamily Caseodontoidea and the newly established order Eugeneodontiformes, in light of the new taxa and characteristics that had been observed since the genus' description.

facts.statement: Ornithoprion's placement in Caseodontidae is based on its bulbous tooth crowns and reduced palatoquadrates, features shared with Caseodus and Erikodus.
facts.quote: Ornithoprions classification within the Caseodontidae is based on the bulbous, rounded nature of its tooth crowns and the reduction of its palatoquadrates, features which are also found in genera such as Caseodus and Erikodus.

facts.statement: While Zangerl's family and order classifications are still used, his view that eugeneodonts are elasmobranchs has been refuted; they are now considered a monophyletic group within Holocephali.
facts.quote: The order and family-level classification established by Zangerl remain in use, although his suggestion that eugeneodonts are elasmobranchs has been refuted by subsequent papers, which find Eugeneodontiformes to be a monophyletic (natural) group in the subclass Holocephali.
